transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, thank you for seeing me. I, um, I actually made this appointment because things have been getting so... complicated at work lately. I'm a jeweler, you see, and I do a lot of custom work and repairs. It's a small shop, very intimate, and I've always prided myself on my customer service. But lately, well, it's just been so frustrating. A customer will come in, right? And they'll ask me a very simple question, something I've answered a thousand times before, like... "When will my ring repair be ready?" And I know the answer, I really do, but when I open my mouth to tell them, it's like my brain just takes off on a completely different track. 

I'll start talking about the repair, but then suddenly I'm talking about the invoices from the supplier, and how they've changed their billing cycle, which reminds me of the new garden soil I bought over the weekend because the bags were stacked exactly like the boxes of ring sizing stock, and then before I know it, I'm going on about my mortgage papers and the interest rates because the numbers just sort of bleed together in my head. And I can see it happening, you know? I can look right at their faces and see them just... losing me. Their eyes sort of glaze over, or they look confused, and I know I'm not making any sense to them, but it's like I can't stop the words from tumbling out all connected like that, even though they shouldn't be. It's just so embarrassing, and it's making it really hard to do my job properly.

When you find yourself going off track in conversation like that, do you still feel like you're talking about something related to the original topic, or does it feel like you completely lose track of what you originally meant to say?

Well, like I was just saying a second ago about the ring repairs and the garden soil... to me, it feels completely, one-hundred-percent related in the moment. It really does! Because, see, when they ask about the ring, I immediately think about the sizing stock we needed for it, which we just ordered. And that supplier's invoice was sitting right on my desk next to my mortgage statement, because I was paying bills on Tuesday morning. Tuesday is usually my quietest day at the shop, you know, so I try to do the business bookkeeping and my personal bills all at the same time to just get it out of the way. 

So the numbers on the invoice and the mortgage interest rate just... they link up in my brain. And the garden soil—well, I bought that over the weekend, and the bags were stacked in the trunk of my car exactly like the boxes of stock in the back room. So in my head, I haven't lost track of the original question at all! I'm just... I'm giving them the whole picture, walking them through the steps of what's going on in my mind to get to the answer. 

But then I look at them, and like I said, I can see them losing me. I can literally watch them checking out, and then it hits me that they just wanted to know if their gold band would be polished and ready to pick up by Friday. But I just can't seem to get straight to 'Friday' without taking this huge, long detour through everything else that feels connected to it in my head. It's like this giant web, and they pull on one little string, and my brain just drags the whole entire web out into the conversation, even though I know they don't need to hear about my soil or my mortgage. I just can't stop the connections from happening out loud.
Do you ever feel like your thoughts are moving faster than usual, like one idea quickly leads to another and another before you can fully finish the first?

Well, no, not really. I wouldn't say they're moving faster than usual, not like a race car or anything. It's not a speed thing, you know? It's more of a... a volume thing, I guess you could say. It's like I have all the time in the world to think them, but there are just so many of them connected together. 

I don't feel like I'm rushing to get the words out before they disappear, or like my brain is buzzing out of control. It's just that when I start on one path, all the side paths look exactly like the main road to me. Like with the jewelry repairs—when I'm sitting at my workbench with my loupe on, looking at a cracked prong on a diamond setting, I'm not thinking fast. I'm actually very methodical. I have to be. I take my time, I assess the metal, I think about the heat I'll need... but then the thought about the heat makes me think about the torch, which makes me think about the gas bill, which makes me think about the mail carrier who always drops the letters on the wet porch. 

And all of those thoughts feel perfectly paced, just like normal thinking, but they're all happening at once and demanding to be said. So it's not that I can't finish the first idea because a new one pushes it out of the way too fast. It's more that I feel like I *have* to finish the first idea by including all the other ideas, because to me, they're all part of the exact same thought. Does that make sense? It's just so frustrating because I know people don't want to hear about the mail carrier when they're asking about their diamond, but to my brain, they aren't separate things moving quickly, they're just one big, slow, tangled ball of yarn.

Once you start talking about something, do you feel a strong need to keep explaining all the connected thoughts until you feel you’ve fully expressed everything, even if you know it might be too much for the listener?

Well, yes, exactly. That's exactly it. It's like... I just have to get it all out so the picture is complete, you know? Like I was saying when I first sat down, I came in because when people ask me a simple question, like when a ring repair will be ready, my answer just starts going from invoices to garden soil to the mortgage papers. And I can see them losing me, I really can. I see their faces just kind of drop, or they look at their watch, or they give me that polite little smile that means 'please stop talking.' 

But even when I see that, it's like I can't just stop in the middle. If I just stopped and said 'Friday,' it would feel like a lie, almost? Or like I'm giving them a half-finished piece of jewelry. You wouldn't hand a customer a ring that's been soldered but not polished, right? You have to finish the whole process. So if I don't explain how the invoice connects to the soil, which connects to the mortgage, which connects to the Tuesday bookkeeping, which is why I know the ring will be ready by Friday... well, the thought just isn't finished. I feel this incredible pressure, just this absolute necessity to lay all the pieces out on the counter so they can see how they fit together, even though my logical brain is screaming at me that they don't care about the mortgage papers. 

I just have to keep going until the whole web is out there. It's exhausting, honestly. I go home at the end of the day and my jaw literally aches from talking, and I just feel so foolish because I know I over-explained everything to everyone who walked through the door. But in the moment, stopping before I've explained every single connection just feels physically impossible.
Do you ever feel like you can’t stop talking, even when you realize that the person listening is clearly uncomfortable or wants you to stop?

Well, no, not really. I mean, it's not like I'm just talking and talking and talking without taking a breath, or like I'm physically unable to close my mouth. It's not a compulsion to just make noise, you know? It's like I was just saying... it's about finishing the thought. 

If I see them getting uncomfortable—and I do, I'm very observant, you have to be in my line of work to read a customer's reaction to a custom piece—if I see them shifting their weight or looking toward the door, I don't feel a need to just keep talking *at* them to hold them hostage. I can stop. I can physically stop speaking. But the problem is, if I stop before I've explained how the garden soil connects to the invoice, the thought isn't done. 

So it's not that I *can't* stop talking, it's that I *shouldn't* stop talking until the explanation is complete, because otherwise, what was the point of starting the explanation in the first place? If I just cut it off, it's like leaving a raw edge on a piece of silver. It's sharp, it's unfinished, it's just... wrong. So I don't feel like I'm out of control of my mouth, I just feel like I'm obligated to finish the puzzle I started, even if they don't want to look at the puzzle anymore. Does that make sense? It's not a runaway train, it's just a very, very long, detailed route that I feel I have to complete.

Have you ever had any experiences or beliefs that other people might find strange or hard to believe, such as feeling like your thoughts are being controlled by outside forces or that you have special powers or abilities?

Well, no, not like special powers or mind control, nothing out of a science fiction movie like that. I don't think anyone is beaming thoughts into my head while I'm at my workbench. But... well, I know it sounds odd, and my husband tells me I'm making a mountain out of a molehill, but lately I've been completely convinced that some of the customers coming into the shop aren't actually there for jewelry at all. 

It started a few months ago when we decided to expand the showroom. We took out a loan, which is where those mortgage papers come in that I was talking about earlier, and it's been stressful. Very stressful. And then suddenly, it seems like certain people are coming in and they just ask so many questions about the new display cases, or the lighting fixtures we chose, or how much square footage we added. They don't even look at the rings! They just wander around the new section, asking all these pointed questions about the renovations. 

My husband says they're just being friendly, just making neighborhood small talk because they noticed the construction, but it doesn't feel like small talk to me. It feels like they're investigating. I really believe they're coming in just to check up on our finances, to see if we've overextended ourselves and if we're going to miss our loan payments. Like they've been sent by the bank, or maybe by competitors, just to gauge if we're going under. 

And I try to explain this to my husband, I tell him, 'Look at how that woman was staring at the new track lighting, she didn't even glance at the sapphire pendants I just finished setting.' But he just sighs and tells me I'm being paranoid. But I'm not paranoid, I'm observant! When you spend thirty years looking at tiny flaws in gemstones through a ten-power loupe, you learn to see things other people miss. You see the little inclusions, the stress fractures. And I see it in these people. They aren't customers. They're checking on our debt. I just know it, even if everyone else thinks it's a strange thing to believe.
Do you ever feel like people are watching or talking about you in ways that others don’t seem to notice, or that events happening around you have special meaning that others don’t understand?

Well, that goes right back to exactly what I was just telling you a moment ago about the shop. That’s exactly it. It’s like they are watching me, or watching the business, in a way that my husband is completely blind to. 

I know I just said it, and I know how odd it sounds when I say it out loud in a doctor's office, but I’ve just gotten so utterly convinced that some of these so-called customers are coming in specifically to check whether I’ll miss my loan payments. And it fits exactly what you're asking, because my husband doesn't see the special meaning in it at all. He’ll be standing right there, wiping down the glass on the new display cases with a microfiber cloth, just chatting away with them. And they’ll be asking all these highly specific questions—not about the cut of a diamond, not about the karat weight of a gold chain, but about the renovations. They want to know who our contractor was, how long the permits took, if the new security gate was expensive. 

To my husband, he just smiles and thinks, 'Oh, they’re only being friendly, just nice neighborhood folks taking an interest.' But I’m sitting there at my jeweler's bench, maybe filing down a prong or something, and I can feel the real intent behind it. I can see them looking around, taking mental notes, doing the math in their heads about what we spent versus what we're bringing in. It’s not just friendly banter. It means something else entirely. They are scrutinizing us. 

And it's so frustrating because I'll wait until the door chimes and they leave, and I'll say to my husband, 'Did you see how they were looking at the lighting fixtures? They're checking up on our debt.' And he just shakes his head and tells me I'm reading into things. But I'm not! I can tell the difference between someone who wants to buy an anniversary gift and someone who is fishing for financial information. It's just... it's so obvious to me, the way they watch us and the questions they ask, but nobody else seems to notice the reality of what's happening right in front of them.
Have you ever felt like the thoughts you're having about these customers or their intentions are being placed in your mind by someone or something outside of yourself?

Oh, no, no, definitely not. Goodness, no. I mean... I know I just went on and on about the customers and the loan, and I know my husband thinks I’m, well, he thinks I'm letting my imagination run wild, but nobody is putting thoughts into my head. It’s not like... like a radio broadcast being beamed in, or some kind of puppet string situation. Not at all. These are absolutely my thoughts. My own observations. 

Like I was saying before about the loupe and the gemstones, when you sit at a jeweler's bench for thirty years, you rely entirely on your own focus. If I'm using a jeweler's saw to cut a really intricate filigree pattern out of a sheet of sterling silver, I have to be completely present in my own mind, or I'll snap the saw blade in half or cut my finger open. So I know my own mind. I know what's mine. 

The thoughts I have about these people coming in to check on the business... they come from my own deductive reasoning. It's just me putting two and two together based on what I'm seeing with my own two eyes. The stress of the expansion loan—which, by the way, we debated for a solid six months before we even signed the first piece of paper, because the interest rates were just all over the place and we had to meet with three different loan officers—that stress is mine. And because I'm the one carrying that worry, I'm the one who is hyper-aware. 

So when that woman came in and spent twenty minutes looking at the track lighting instead of the sapphire pendants, my brain—*my* brain, nobody else's—makes the connection. It's just me being vigilant. I wish I *could* blame it on an outside force, honestly, because then maybe I could just turn it off and not worry about the mortgage all night! But no, it's all me. Just my own mind working overtime, putting the pieces together based on what's happening right in front of me.

doctor.question: Have you ever had any experiences or beliefs that other people might find strange or hard to believe, such as feeling like your thoughts are being controlled by outside forces or that you have special powers or abilities?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know it sounds odd, but I’ve gotten convinced some customers are coming in just to check whether I’ll miss payments, because they ask too many questions about the new showroom even after my husband says they’re only being friendly.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about strange or hard to believe experiences or beliefs, such as thoughts being controlled or having special powers, which screens for delusions.

patient.answer:
Well, no, not like special powers or mind control, nothing out of a science fiction movie like that. I don't think anyone is beaming thoughts into my head while I'm at my workbench. But... well, I know it sounds odd, and my husband tells me I'm making a mountain out of a molehill, but lately I've been completely convinced that some of the customers coming into the shop aren't actually there for jewelry at all. 

It started a few months ago when we decided to expand the showroom. We took out a loan, which is where those mortgage papers come in that I was talking about earlier, and it's been stressful. Very stressful. And then suddenly, it seems like certain people are coming in and they just ask so many questions about the new display cases, or the lighting fixtures we chose, or how much square footage we added. They don't even look at the rings! They just wander around the new section, asking all these pointed questions about the renovations. 

My husband says they're just being friendly, just making neighborhood small talk because they noticed the construction, but it doesn't feel like small talk to me. It feels like they're investigating. I really believe they're coming in just to check up on our finances, to see if we've overextended ourselves and if we're going to miss our loan payments. Like they've been sent by the bank, or maybe by competitors, just to gauge if we're going under. 

And I try to explain this to my husband, I tell him, 'Look at how that woman was staring at the new track lighting, she didn't even glance at the sapphire pendants I just finished setting.' But he just sighs and tells me I'm being paranoid. But I'm not paranoid, I'm observant! When you spend thirty years looking at tiny flaws in gemstones through a ten-power loupe, you learn to see things other people miss. You see the little inclusions, the stress fractures. And I see it in these people. They aren't customers. They're checking on our debt. I just know it, even if everyone else thinks it's a strange thing to believe.

doctor.question: Do you ever feel like people are watching or talking about you in ways that others don’t seem to notice, or that events happening around you have special meaning that others don’t understand?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know it sounds odd, but I’ve gotten convinced some customers are coming in just to check whether I’ll miss payments, because they ask too many questions about the new showroom even after my husband says they’re only being friendly.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about ideas of reference and paranoia, which are types of delusions.

patient.answer:
Well, that goes right back to exactly what I was just telling you a moment ago about the shop. That’s exactly it. It’s like they are watching me, or watching the business, in a way that my husband is completely blind to. 

I know I just said it, and I know how odd it sounds when I say it out loud in a doctor's office, but I’ve just gotten so utterly convinced that some of these so-called customers are coming in specifically to check whether I’ll miss my loan payments. And it fits exactly what you're asking, because my husband doesn't see the special meaning in it at all. He’ll be standing right there, wiping down the glass on the new display cases with a microfiber cloth, just chatting away with them. And they’ll be asking all these highly specific questions—not about the cut of a diamond, not about the karat weight of a gold chain, but about the renovations. They want to know who our contractor was, how long the permits took, if the new security gate was expensive. 

To my husband, he just smiles and thinks, 'Oh, they’re only being friendly, just nice neighborhood folks taking an interest.' But I’m sitting there at my jeweler's bench, maybe filing down a prong or something, and I can feel the real intent behind it. I can see them looking around, taking mental notes, doing the math in their heads about what we spent versus what we're bringing in. It’s not just friendly banter. It means something else entirely. They are scrutinizing us. 

And it's so frustrating because I'll wait until the door chimes and they leave, and I'll say to my husband, 'Did you see how they were looking at the lighting fixtures? They're checking up on our debt.' And he just shakes his head and tells me I'm reading into things. But I'm not! I can tell the difference between someone who wants to buy an anniversary gift and someone who is fishing for financial information. It's just... it's so obvious to me, the way they watch us and the questions they ask, but nobody else seems to notice the reality of what's happening right in front of them.

inference.note: The patient reports experiences of being observed or scrutinized by others (customers) in a way that others (e.g., husband) do not confirm, and the belief that certain individuals are monitoring the business’s financial status. This suggests the presence of delusional themes or ideas that may be indicative of a delusional disorder or other persistent delusional disorders (F22, F23.x). Schizophrenic spectrum disorders (F20.x) are less supported due to absence of formal thought disorder, disorganized speech, or other core features of schizophrenia.

doctor.question: Have you ever felt like the thoughts you're having about these customers or their intentions are being placed in your mind by someone or something outside of yourself?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about thought insertion, which is not part of my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Oh, no, no, definitely not. Goodness, no. I mean... I know I just went on and on about the customers and the loan, and I know my husband thinks I’m, well, he thinks I'm letting my imagination run wild, but nobody is putting thoughts into my head. It’s not like... like a radio broadcast being beamed in, or some kind of puppet string situation. Not at all. These are absolutely my thoughts. My own observations. 

Like I was saying before about the loupe and the gemstones, when you sit at a jeweler's bench for thirty years, you rely entirely on your own focus. If I'm using a jeweler's saw to cut a really intricate filigree pattern out of a sheet of sterling silver, I have to be completely present in my own mind, or I'll snap the saw blade in half or cut my finger open. So I know my own mind. I know what's mine. 

The thoughts I have about these people coming in to check on the business... they come from my own deductive reasoning. It's just me putting two and two together based on what I'm seeing with my own two eyes. The stress of the expansion loan—which, by the way, we debated for a solid six months before we even signed the first piece of paper, because the interest rates were just all over the place and we had to meet with three different loan officers—that stress is mine. And because I'm the one carrying that worry, I'm the one who is hyper-aware. 

So when that woman came in and spent twenty minutes looking at the track lighting instead of the sapphire pendants, my brain—*my* brain, nobody else's—makes the connection. It's just me being vigilant. I wish I *could* blame it on an outside force, honestly, because then maybe I could just turn it off and not worry about the mortgage all night! But no, it's all me. Just my own mind working overtime, putting the pieces together based on what's happening right in front of me.
